name: Mike Kelly
rtf_details:
{"ops":[{"insert":"Jackson County Amateur Radio is participating in Winter Field Day 25th-26th January 2025 at the Stevenson City Park Pavilion ("},{"attributes":{"link":"https://maps.app.goo.gl/avemEiYvC8vv8qvb8"},"insert":"https://maps.app.goo.gl/avemEiYvC8vv8qvb8"},{"insert":"). Our goal is to operate up to three stations for up to 30 hours.

JCAR will hold an amateur radio exam session prior to WFD, starting at 0900 25 January 2024. Setup begins at 0800. WFD starts at 1000 and goes until 1559 26 January 2024. Tear down will begin no later than 1600. All times are CST. Even if you aren’t interested in operating, your presence is greatly appreciated during setup, tear down, and throughout field day if you want to learn more about field operations. You do not have to be a club member or even a licensed amateur to be part of WFD.

If you want to camp overnight, the city of Stevenson charges $30 per campsite with water and electricity. A couple of club members will likely reserve a couple campsites for others to use.

We will be operating outdoors. You should bring space heaters, either electric, kerosene, propane, any that don’t use an open flame. We will have a designated warming area for the safety of those out there in case someone gets too cold. Dress according to the weather and you will most likely have a very comfortable and enjoyable experience.

If you want to bring any off-grid power sources, WFD is the perfect time to try them out. It’s okay if they fail. We will have outlets available.

We will be using K4SCO exclusively during WFD. Operators will use networked computer logging unless there's an equipment failure. Only then can you log using any method they choose, but the logs must be legible and must contain all required WFD information: Call sign, class, category, location identifier, frequency, date, and UTC time. Familiarize yourself with the WFD rules here: https://winterfieldday.org/sop.php

Please be respectful of the operators while they are making contacts. If you want to talk to an operator, be patient and wait until they have a free moment. If you want to hang out and have a conversation, please take it somewhere away from the operators. You’ll be asked to leave if you repeatedly distract or interfere with an operator.

There will be food and beverages if you bring them. There will likely be coffee, water, sodas, and snacks brought for all by the operators. Want grilled meats? Bring a grill and meats. Bring your smoker and get a nice brisket going. There are several places to eat nearby, and anywhere that delivers food will most likely deliver to the park.
One of the most important things you can do if you can’t make it out to Winter Field Day at all is to make contact with our stations. You help the operators and the club by working the club once per band and mode.
"}]}

{"ops":[{"insert":"Austin VE7QH, Mike VE7KPZ, and friends will operate from Cec's cabin 8km (16km round trip) by ski or snowshoe into the Larch Hills Nordic Society cross-country ski area. While the tiny cabin will be full of our bodies overnight, we do welcome guests to stop in and check out the action in the daytime (and guests operate if a current RAC member (please bring your RAC member number along for our records)).

We will most likely be a three-radio setup with a hex beam for the HF higher bands and EFHW for the HF lower bands. We will employ a variety of VHF/UHF antennas for 2m/70cm and satellite operations. We will cover all modes (CW, phone, and digital) on most bands. The one objective we won't meet is running QRP, as with the VE7RAC call, we need to be able to hold a frequency when calling (which we will be doing most of the time).

If you are in good physical shape and can take care of yourself (clothing, food, water) outside for an extended period of time in the winter, come visit us for the day. If you plan to attend, perhaps let us know ahead of the event—email Mike at ve7kpz@gmail.com.

rtf_details:
{"ops":[{"insert":"I am completely new to POTA. I've been a Tech for less than a year. Not sure what to expect, so any/all suggestions are truly appreciated. 

In the spirit of off-site, emergency communications, I'll be tent-camping at Raptor Ridge and self-contained.  I'll be using batteries, solar panels and a generator for everything RF-related. But, cheating a bit, I will have electric heaters in the tent and canopy!

I'm planning to operate on 2M, 1.25M and 70cm using two different HTs and two or three separate antennas.
I have some work to do to build a list of Simplex frequencies as I've only used repeaters thus far. 
Again, suggestions?

I've not done any organized logging of contacts. Is there an approved PPRAA form and format? 
I could really use advise here, but I may learn by observation at Winterfest. 
I've read the best practices document, but it (rightfully) reads as guidelines for more experienced operators.

I am also planning to use a RTL-SDR/Raspberry Pi5 with a Mag Loop antenna to view lower frequencies. 
And I might bring a Realistic DX-390 to listen to SW bands I can't demodulate with the SDR.

It's easy to make these plans without prior experience! Aha! 
So, I am eager to hear your comments and suggestions!

Best Regards, Merry Christmas and Happy New Year to all!
Greg Hill
KF0OZT

"}]}

{"ops":[{"attributes":{"color":"#1f1f1f"},"insert":"PRARC Winter Field Day 2025: Grit, Gratitude, and Game Plan"},{"insert":"

The on-going firestorm in Los Angeles serves as a stark reminder of why we do what we do. When disaster strikes, amateur radio steps up—reliable, resilient, and ready to serve. That’s why this Winter Field Day is about more than just making contacts; it’s about sharpening our edge and proving we’re battle-ready when the call comes.

Last week, we hit some major milestones, and it’s all thanks to a crew that knows how to dig deep and deliver. Let’s take a moment to recognize the team going above and beyond:

Mike, K6AJ: Antenna Coordinator—getting us on the air, no matter the terrain.
Scott, NS7C: Media Team Co-captain—crafting the story of our mission.
Randy, KO6DJI: Mobile Tower and Generator Coordinator—powering up our ops.
Glen, KD6HJR: Mobile Tower and Generator Co-coordinator—keeping us running.
Eric, KN6EIV: Coax Coordinator—making sure every connection is solid.
John, KN6TCG: CERT Trailer Coordinator and Media Team Captain—holding it all together.
Bob, KB6CIO: Refreshment Coordinator—fueling the team for the long haul.
Your grit, your time, and your selfless commitment to PRARC and emergency communications don’t go unnoticed. You’re the backbone of this operation.

Now, as we gear up for January 25th, here’s where we stand:
We still need a Social Media Coordinator—someone with the chops to bring our operation to life in real time, maybe even live stream the action. John, KN6TCG, is also working with local media outlets to amplify our reach, just like summer Field Day.

{"ops":[{"insert":"Winter Field Day is an event for Amateur Radio Operators to setup a remote site to practice emergency radio communications should all infrastructure fails and power/cell communications shut down like what happened when Hurricane Helene devastated North Carolina. It is volunteer operators like these that conduct rescue operations and call in aid for food, water, medical supplies and power generators to help victims of these kind of tragedies. 

Winter Field Day is a say to practice emergency communications in dangerous conditions that adds freezing temperatures, ice, snow and other hazardous conditions to enhance the training opportunities to improve disaster preparedness through these adverse conditions. We will be conducting voice and digital communications to send messages throughout the world to achieve specific objectives to further the expertise in supporting the region should disasters occur. Multiple transceivers and various antennas will be used to achieve each objective. All equipment will be powered by battery, solar or power generator to simulate the loss of electricity.

We welcome the public to come out and see what these volunteers do installing communications via VHF, UHF, HF and satellite communications. Feel free to reach out to our site coordinator at KL5TY.Alaska@gmail.com.

rtf_details:
{"ops":[{"insert":"Next Event: January 25from 1900z (2pm Eastern) to January 26 1900z (2pm Eastern), 2025
 
Winter Field Day is sponsored by the Winter Field Day Association (WFDA), a dedicated group of Amateur Radio Operators who believe that emergency communications in a winter environment is just as important as the preparations and practice that is done each summer but with some additional unique operational concerns. Full information about this exciting event can be found at www.winterfieldday.com.
 
The W4DOC 2025 Winter Field Day event will take place from 2pm January 25th through 2pm January 26th, 2025 at Sweetwater
Creek State Park. The address is 1750 Mt Vernon Rd, Lithia Springs, GA 30122.

If you’re a GPS aficionado it’s 33.75733, -84.63857 for the Park Office and 33.758659, -84.641137 for the campground location. For those using thw WhatThreeWords app: tombstone.assume.splashes
We are not a hardcore contesting group, we do this to have fun and play with radios, no regimented signups for this event. The W4DOC Social Committee will once again provide supper beginning around 5:30pm, for those who operate overnight, coffee, water, snacks, and soda throughout. We’ll have enough for all who join us.

This is a state park so you are expected to stop by the park office across the street from the entrance to the campground and pay a small $5 entry fee. There will be a gate code to access campground area provided by the club. There is a flyer with a small map attached to this email.
 
If you want to try out amateur radio, see what the ARC club is all about, enjoy good radio fellowship, you are invited to join us for great radio, food and company.

rtf_details:
{"ops":[{"insert":"We invite folks to brave the cold and and drop by to see us. We will have the clubhouse open, typically from about 9 AM until usually 10 or 11 PM, depending on the weather. We don't often get a lot of visitors because of the weather and no events at the fair, but club members have a great time with it.

Right now, our clubhouse is at the Scout Cabin in the Jay County Fairgrounds (on the west side of the fairgrounds...a log cabin that's hard to miss), but we will be relocating to another building soon that will be for exclusive use of our club and its members.

name: Scott Gaudet
rtf_details:
{"ops":[{"insert":"The Boston Amateur Radio Club is thrilled to announce that we'll once again be heading to the AMC Ponkapoag in Massachusetts for a weekend of amateur radio fun! We've snagged three cozy cabins (yes, you read that right - COZY CABINS!) and will be setting up shop from Friday, January 24th to Sunday at 2pm.

Now, we know what you're thinking... "What about parking?" Don't worry, fellow hams! While parking might be a bit of a challenge, the scenic hike in is totally worth it. And who needs a driveway when you can enjoy the beautiful winter trails?

This isn't just any ordinary contest - it's Winter Field Day 2025! We're not just about winning (although, let's be real, we'll try our best to take home some prizes). We're about camaraderie, friendly competition, Learning new things, and most import preparation of our gear in the field while making new friends over a shared love of amateur radio.

So mark your calendars, grab your gear, and get ready for an unforgettable weekend in the woods! Visitors are welcome - just be prepared for a hike. And remember: even though it's a contest, we're all here to have FUN!

See you there, hams!
"}]}

name: Rob Zingarelli
rtf_details:
{"ops":[{"insert":"Once again, W4ZNG and whoever the heck else wants to show up will be at Wright Lake in the Apalachicola National Forest off of SR 65, at the very northern edge of Franklin County.  This probably includes the Tate's Heck Amateur Radio Club (THARC), but being a highly informal group, it's hard to speak for the other members.

To get there from Hwy 98: Turn north on SR 65, then after 22 miles, turn left onto Wright Lake Road (it's a dirt road, but well maintained).  At about a mile and a half, turn right onto the campground road (it's well marked).  Enter the campground loop and look for an old blue F-150 and a bunch of antennas.  (note: there is no "Wright Lake Road" sign, but it is two miles past the Fort Gadsden sign)

The extended weather forecast looks good but, being tent-based campers, we do reserve the right to curtail operations if the weather turns truly awful.  (We're in this for the cool weather fun, not to prove ourselves in inclement weather – we'll save that for hurricane season!)  If there are any last-minute changes in plans, we'll post them at the website link.  The plan is to set up on Friday mid-day, be on the air at start time, and then operate into Sunday afternoon, leaving time to break camp and get home well before sunset.

We should be operating on HF on 80m-10m, as well as 6m, 2m, and 70cm – if the tropoducting conditions smile upon the atmosphere during the event.  All on solar power, of course.  Cell phone service at the site is almost non-existent, but we will monitor 146.52 as a talk-in frequency.

Bring your own coffee cup (though we may have some spares), and any gear you might want – especially camping gear if you're staying.  Campsites at the Nat. Forest campground are $20/night.  Breakfasts will be eggs and spam, and feel free to BYOG (bring your own grits).
"}]}

name: Ted Berzinski, Hamars Vice-president
rtf_details:
{"ops":[{"insert":"The High Appalachian Mountain Amateur Radio Society, or HAMARS for short, has perhaps as its highest priority to help amateur radio operators improve their preparedness for disasters and enhance their operational abilities.  And club members see Field Days as the organization's primary crucible for accomplishing this goal.

January 25-26, 2025 will be the sixth consecutive year that the HAMARS club will be participating in Winter Field Day, and the third consecutive year at the Smith Creek Road location.  We will be fielding multiple stations at the site, each with its own transceiver, antenna and logging computer, and the communications equipment will be run 100% on alternative power.  There are several sites within a few hundred feet of each other where these stations will be based.  

The headquarters site--on loan to us from a wonderful neighbor--is an unheated single wide trailer which is used in the warmer months for processing honey from nearby hives, and for canning produce grown in local gardens.  This building, which we have named "The Honey House" is at the geographical coordinates on the map, easily seen just off the south side of Smith Creek Road.

This particular area is known to be cold and snowy in wintertime.  There's six inches of snow on the ground right now, and there's a commercial ski resort just a mile away.  For the early part of the week preceding Winter Field Day, the forecast for that location is daily highs in the single digits to low teens (Fahrenheit), with nighttime lows in the single digits to below zero.  So if you come and visit--and all are welcome--be sure to dress warmly!

If you want to stop by, the best time would be on Saturday, January 25, between 12 Noon and 4 pm Eastern Time.  While we'll be setting up before this time segment and operating into Sunday morning, our availability to be able to talk with you will be hit or miss.
"}]}
